opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's less of a concern for me than people might expect, and I think that's because I've spent a lot of time actually on factory floors rather than just looking at the demos.

The first thing I'd say is that the framing of "replacing" workers misses what's really happening in manufacturing right now. Most of the plants I talk to can't find enough people. They've got open positions they can't fill, they've got an aging workforce that's retiring, and younger people frankly aren't lining up to do repetitive, physically punishing work for eight or ten hours a day. So in a lot of cases, the robot isn't taking someone's job. It's filling a job that's been sitting empty for months.

The second thing is that the jobs humanoids are realistically going to do first are the dull, dirty, and dangerous ones: lifting heavy totes, moving parts between stations, working in extreme heat or around hazardous materials. Those are the tasks that cause injuries and burnout. If we can take those off people's plates, that's a good outcome.

Now, I don't want to be naive about it. There will be disruption, and some roles will change or go away. Where I think we have a real responsibility, as an industry and as a society, is in the transition. That means investing in training so the person who used to carry boxes can become the person who supervises, maintains, or programs the robots. Those jobs exist and they pay better, but nobody gets there automatically. Companies deploying this technology need to bring their workforce along with them, not just cut headcount and call it efficiency.

So my concern isn't really the robots themselves. It's whether we handle the human side of the transition thoughtfully. If we do that well, I think workers come out ahead.

r001.rationale: The candidate says robots can fill vacancies and take on dull, dirty, or dangerous tasks, but does not frame repetitive factory jobs as jobs that belong to robots.

r002.rationale: It mentions unfilled positions, but does not explain that automation enables businesses to expand and thereby create employment.

r003.rationale: It names roles supervising, maintaining, or programming robots, but does not say new technological capabilities enable entirely new kinds of human work.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, not in the way most people assume. I've spent a lot of time on factory floors, and the reality is that manufacturers in the US and Europe can't fill the jobs they already have. There are hundreds of thousands of open positions, and the workforce is aging out faster than young people are coming in. So the first wave of humanoids isn't walking in and taking someone's job. It's filling a shift nobody wanted, or doing the task that's been injuring people for decades: the repetitive lifting, the awkward reaches, the work at the end of a line where you're standing in the same spot for ten hours.

What does concern me is the framing of "replacement" as the goal. When a company buys a robot purely to cut headcount, they usually get a worse outcome than the company that asks, "What's the part of this job a human is bad at or shouldn't be doing?" The best deployments I've seen pair the robot with the worker. The person becomes the one who handles exceptions, does quality checks, and supervises a small fleet. That's a better job, and it tends to pay more.

The other piece I'd flag is timing. Humanoids are improving fast, but general-purpose dexterity in a messy, real factory is still hard. We're years away from a robot that can walk onto any line and do whatever a person does. That gives us a window to get the transition right: training, redeployment, being honest with workers about what's coming. The risk isn't the technology itself. It's that we waste that window and then act surprised.

r001.rationale: The response says humanoids can take on repetitive, injury-prone tasks that people should not have to do, framing those tasks as better suited to robots.

r002.rationale: It discusses unfilled jobs and robot-worker partnerships, but does not explain that automation can create employment by enabling businesses to expand.

r003.rationale: It describes workers handling exceptions, quality checks, and robot supervision, but does not connect new technological capabilities to entirely new kinds of human work.

astra-6.text: It does concern me. If you’re a factory worker and you hear that a robot could do your job, that’s a very real threat to your livelihood. I don’t think we should dismiss that. At the same time, there are dangerous, repetitive tasks where getting a person out of harm’s way would be a good thing. The question is how we make that transition. Are we giving workers a chance to learn new skills and move into other roles, or are we simply cutting costs and leaving them behind? I’m excited about what robots could do, but we have to take responsibility for what that means for people.

r001.rationale: It calls some repetitive tasks dangerous and says robots could take them on, but does not frame those jobs as belonging to robots.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that automation can create jobs by allowing businesses to expand.

r003.rationale: It mentions retraining and moving into other roles, but does not say new technological capabilities enable entirely new kinds of human work.

sol-6.1.text: It does concern me, particularly for the people whose livelihoods depend on those jobs. But I think we need to distinguish between replacing a person and automating a task. If a robot can take on dangerous, repetitive work, that can be a real benefit. The harder question is what happens to the worker afterward. Are we helping them move into a better role, or simply cutting costs and leaving them behind? That transition deserves as much attention as the technology itself.
